# Reading NUMA Topology without numactl

## Thesis

**NUMA** (Non-Uniform Memory Access) means memory attached to one socket is faster for CPUs on that socket. Before you pin threads or blame "memory latency", read the topology. You do not need `numactl` for a first look: sysfs under `/sys/devices/system/node/` and `/proc/zoneinfo` are enough. This chapter inspects a single-node VM and shows what multi-node output would add.

## Mental model

```text
  node0: CPUs 0-7, local DRAM
  node1: CPUs 8-15, local DRAM
       cross-node load → higher latency / lower bandwidth
```

## Worked examples

`numactl` is **not** installed here (and we will not install packages for a chapter). Read-only sysfs:

```bash
ls /sys/devices/system/node/
cat /sys/devices/system/node/node0/meminfo | head
cat /sys/devices/system/node/node0/cpulist
head -40 /proc/zoneinfo
```

Output (trimmed) from this run:

```
has_cpu
has_generic_initiator
has_memory
has_normal_memory
node0
online
possible
power
uevent
== node0 ==
Node 0 MemTotal:       16386368 kB
Node 0 MemFree:         5183212 kB
Node 0 MemUsed:        11203156 kB
Node 0 SwapCached:            0 kB
Node 0 Active:          1525412 kB
Node 0 Inactive:        5364312 kB
Node 0 Active(anon):       1372 kB
Node 0 Inactive(anon):  3180496 kB
cpus: 0-7

```

This guest is **one NUMA node** (`node0`, CPUs `0-7`, ~16 GiB). That is normal for small VMs — the skill is confirming it before applying multi-node tuning guides.

## Trap

**Copying `numactl --interleave=all` folklore onto a single-node machine.** Interleave policies matter when remote memory is real. On one node they add complexity without benefit.

## Boring rule

Always print `node*/cpulist` and `MemTotal` before changing CPU affinity or memory policy. Install `numactl` only on machines you own when you need `numactl --hardware` pretty-printing.

## Try this

1. On a dual-socket host, compare `node0/distance` and `node1/distance`.
2. Use `lscpu` NUMA lines next to sysfs.
3. Read `numa(7)`.
